transcript:
Header: 2026-05-05 10:00 PDT | Duration: 45 mins | Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Liam O'Neill (Redwood CSM), Carlos Ruiz (Acme Infra), Priya Nambiar (Acme ML), Evan Lee (Acme CTO), Sara Kim (Acme Product)

[10:00] Jordan Park: hey everyone good morning thanks for joining um we'll kick off, this is our weekly latency tune check-in. quick agenda — TTFT numbers, streaming results, seq length profiles, and kernel choices then next steps, ok?
[10:01] Carlos Ruiz: Yep thanks Jordan, quick note — we've been getting p95 spikes on our staging endpoints when traffic bursts, so keen to see TTFT improvements.
[10:02] Maya Chen: cool, I have the microbench results up, i ran the two candidate models with and without streaming and with different kernel flags, note these are local infra sims not dedicated yet so numbers will change a bit.
[10:03] Priya Nambiar: when you say streaming, do you mean server-side chunked streaming or our app-level polling?
[10:03] Maya Chen: server-side chunked streaming — where we flush token batches as they're generated; that reduces TTFT but can slightly increase tail on very short responses due to extra per-chunk overhead.
[10:04] Evan Lee: hmm ok we care a lot about TTFT for our user flows (first token to UI), p50 matters more than p99 for chat, but for compliance workflows p99 is critical.
[10:05] Maya Chen: noted. so baseline — model A (open-llama-13b-quant) and model B (gpt-ish-7b-quant) on a V100-like sim; sequence lengths tested: 512, 1024, 2048, 4096. continuous batching was disabled to measure single-request TTFT.
[10:06] Maya Chen: results: model A TTFT 512 seq = ~120ms, 1024 = ~160ms, 2048 = ~220ms, 4096 = ~360ms. model B TTFT 512 = ~95ms, 1024 = 130ms, 2048 = 190ms, 4096 = 300ms. streaming reduced TTFT by ~30-40% on average for both but increased p99 by ~10-15ms in some configs.
[10:07] Carlos Ruiz: those look promising — can you break out which kernel config gave that; you mentioned kernel selection earlier?
[10:07] Maya Chen: yeah so we tried two kernel paths: default fused-attn and an experimental flash-attn variant; flash-attn reduced per-token latency especially for long sequences, for model A we saw ~15% improvement at 2048+, for model B it's a bit less pronounced. However the flash-attn path has a higher memory footprint and some instability on 12GB GPUs.
[10:08] Priya Nambiar: instability how severe? crashes or just OOM margins?
[10:08] Maya Chen: more like OOM margins and occasional kernel fallbacks — Redwood runtime can auto-fallback to fused path but that causes a single-request hiccup. we logged 2 fallbacks in a 10k request sim under burst.
[10:09] Jordan Park: just to be explicit — the runtime's smart routing can route heavier requests to larger model variants or different kernel profiles when it detects memory pressure; fallback is graceful but you'll see a spike. that's why we recommend a canary with your actual traffic profile.
[10:10] Carlos Ruiz: right. that's our ask — can you run the canary on a traffic snapshot? we'll share a CSV.
[10:10] Jordan Park: absolutely, that's on the next steps.
[10:11] Liam O'Neill: quick note about quantization and kernel combos — aggressive quantization (4-bit) gives cost win but increases latency variance for certain ops, especially on older GPUs. we suggested 8-bit with per-channel quant where latency stability is the priority.
[10:12] Priya Nambiar: for our compliance pipelines we may accept slightly higher cost for stability. do you have concrete guidance on batching and cache settings?
[10:12] Maya Chen: yes — KV cache hit is huge for multi-turn chat; if your average conversation length is >800 tokens, the cache reduces effective compute per token dramatically. batching: for latency SLOs we keep max batch small (<=8) and use dynamic batching with a per-route cutoff. for throughput jobs you can bump batch size.
[10:13] Evan Lee: our median conv length is around 1.2k tokens, so cache should help. but our spike traffic patterns cause brief queues — any tips for avoiding queue-induced p99 spikes?
[10:14] Maya Chen: concurrency limits and admission control — set a concurrency cap per route tied to your CPU/GPU concurrency; Redwood Dedicated can reserve capacity so bursts don't queue on shared pool. also prefix caching for repeated prompts helps.
[10:15] Carlos Ruiz: curious about streaming vs TTFT tradeoff — you said streaming lowers TTFT but might raise p99. can you explain in lay terms?
[10:15] Maya Chen: sure — streaming sends partial tokens earlier, so the user sees first byte faster. but streaming requires extra flushes and memory copies and can prevent some kernel amortizations; under heavy load that overhead can add to tail. non-streaming waits until a chunk is bigger so per-token amortization is better but first byte delayed.
[10:16] Sara Kim: for product, first byte matters for perception — we prefer streaming for chat UIs. for batch workflows we won't use streaming.
[10:17] Jordan Park: another lever is hybrid: stream small prompts, non-stream large completions. Redwood supports per-route streaming toggles.
[10:18] Priya Nambiar: what about model fallbacks — if flash-attn fails, will it fall back automatically and keep context?
[10:19] Maya Chen: yes runtime will fallback to compatible kernel, KV cache remains intact. the only user-visible effect is a latency hiccup for that request; we also capture telemetry so you can correlate fallbacks to p99 events.
[10:20] Evan Lee: telemetry's important for us — need to tie to our observability stack. do you support sending traces or logs to our splunk?
[10:21] Jordan Park: yes we have tracing hooks and can forward logs or use s3/secure endpoints; we'll include the integration doc in the security packet.
[10:22] Carlos Ruiz: security question — when you talk about dedicated, is data ever accessible by other tenants? we need strict isolation.
[10:22] Jordan Park: Dedicated is hardware-isolated for your tenant, and for Private we can do VPC/on-prem. we'll attach SOC2 docs and network diagrams.
[10:23] Carlos Ruiz: great. one more — what's the expected TTFT improvement moving from our staging infra to Redwood dedicated G4dn/G5-class?
[10:23] Maya Chen: ballpark — you should see TTFT reduce 20-40% depending on the model and sequence length; flash-attn on G5 gives more gains for long sequences. exact numbers we'll provide after we run the dedicated baseline.
[10:24] Priya Nambiar: can you share the kernel selection spreadsheet?
[10:24] Jordan Park: yes we'll send it — includes recommended kernel flags by model, seq length sweet spots, memory footprints and fallback notes.
[10:25] Maya Chen: and i'll attach the raw microbench CSVs from today's runs.
[10:26] Carlos Ruiz: ok thanks. curious about continuous batching — you disabled it for TTFT, but would you enable it in prod?
[10:26] Maya Chen: for prod we enable adaptive batching — it yields better throughput and slightly higher TTFT median, but we tune queueing windows to meet your SLO. for chat routes we bias low latency, for bulk generation we bias throughput.
[10:28] Evan Lee: sounds good. any blockers from Redwood side to run the canary?
[10:28] Jordan Park: just the traffic snapshot and a short VIP whitelist for the canary endpoints. also we may need a small dedicated pool for the baseline run which we'll propose in the pricing doc.
[10:29] Carlos Ruiz: will send traffic snapshot and whitelist by 2026-05-07.
[10:30] Sara Kim: recap please?
[10:30] Jordan Park: recap — Maya will run TTFT + streaming microbenchmarks across 512/1k/2k/4k seqs for the two candidate models and share CSVs by 2026-05-08; Jordan will send dedicated capacity pricing and kernel-selection spreadsheet by 2026-05-06; Carlos to share traffic CSV and SLOs by 2026-05-07; schedule dedicated baseline for 2026-05-12 pending you confirm whitelist. Redwood will include SOC2/network docs.
[10:31] Carlos Ruiz: thanks everyone, that timeline works.
[10:32] Jordan Park: great thanks all, we'll follow up in email with artifacts and calendar invites, bye.
